title: What is the difference between the Kubernetes `RollingUpdate` and `Recreate` deployment strategies (zero-downtime at the cost of extra pods/memory vs guaranteed downtime), and when would you choose each?
shortTitle: Kubernetes `RollingUpdate` vs `Recreate` deployment strategies — trade-offs and when to choose each

s1_definition.profdef: `RollingUpdate` and `Recreate` are the two built-in strategies a Kubernetes Deployment uses to replace old pods with new ones during an update. `RollingUpdate` gradually replaces old pods with new pods a few at a time, keeping some old pods serving traffic while new pods start, which achieves zero downtime at the cost of briefly running extra pods and running two versions simultaneously. `Recreate` first terminates every old pod and only then starts the new pods, which guarantees a window of downtime but guarantees that exactly one version runs at any moment. You tune `RollingUpdate` with `maxSurge`, how many extra pods above the desired count are allowed, and `maxUnavailable`, how many pods may be missing during the roll.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India needs to replace all the tellers at a branch with newly trained tellers. The rolling approach sends in one new teller while the old ones keep serving customers, then swaps them one by one, so the queue never stops — but for a while there are more tellers than desks. The recreate approach closes the branch, sends everyone home, brings in the new tellers, and reopens — nobody is served during the swap, but there is never any confusion about who is on duty.
s1_definition.oneliner: RollingUpdate keeps the lights on by overlapping two versions; Recreate turns the lights off so only one version ever runs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `RollingUpdate` and `Recreate` are the two built-in strategies a Kubernetes Deployment uses to replace old pods with new ones during an update. `RollingUpdate` gradually replaces old pods with new pods a few at a time, keeping some old pods serving traffic while new pods start, which achieves zero downtime at the cost of briefly running extra pods and running two versions simultaneously. `Recreate` first terminates every old pod and only then starts the new pods, which guarantees a window of downtime but guarantees that exactly one version runs at any moment. You tune `RollingUpdate` with `maxSurge`, how many extra pods above the desired count are allowed, and `maxUnavailable`, how many pods may be missing during the roll.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India needs to replace all the tellers at a branch with newly trained tellers. The rolling approach sends in one new teller while the old ones keep serving customers, then swaps them one by one, so the queue never stops — but for a while there are more tellers than desks. The recreate approach closes the branch, sends everyone home, brings in the new tellers, and reopens — nobody is served during the swap, but there is never any confusion about who is on duty.

**One line to remember:** RollingUpdate keeps the lights on by overlapping two versions; Recreate turns the lights off so only one version ever runs.

sections.s2_technical:
A Kubernetes Deployment manages a set of identical pods through a ReplicaSet. When you change the pod template, for example by pointing at a new container image version, the Deployment must replace the old pods with new ones, and the `strategy.type` field decides how.

With `RollingUpdate`, which is the default, Kubernetes replaces pods incrementally. Two parameters shape the roll. `maxSurge` says how many pods above the desired replica count may exist temporarily; if you want ten pods and set `maxSurge` to twenty-five percent, Kubernetes may run up to thirteen pods during the transition. `maxUnavailable` says how many pods below the desired count may be unavailable at once; if set to twenty-five percent, at least eight of the ten must always be ready. The practical effect is that Kubernetes spins up new pods, waits for them to pass their readiness probe, shifts traffic to them, and only then tears down old pods. Because old pods keep serving until new pods are healthy, users experience no interruption. The costs are that you temporarily consume extra memory and CPU for the surge pods, and critically, two versions of your application run at the same time, so both versions must be compatible with the same database schema and the same messages on the queue.

With `Recreate`, Kubernetes scales the old ReplicaSet all the way down to zero, waits for every old pod to terminate, and only then scales the new ReplicaSet up. During the gap between the last old pod dying and the first new pod becoming ready, the service has no running pods and requests fail. The benefit is simplicity and safety of a different kind: there is never a moment when two versions coexist. This matters when the new version is fundamentally incompatible with the old, such as a change that migrates the data in a way the old code cannot read, or a singleton process that must not run twice, like a job scheduler that would double-process if two versions overlapped.

Choosing between them is about whether your application can tolerate two versions running together and whether you can tolerate downtime. Choose `RollingUpdate` for stateless, backward-compatible services such as a customer-facing API where downtime is unacceptable and the new version is compatible with the old during the overlap. Choose `Recreate` when two versions absolutely cannot coexist, when the service holds an exclusive resource, or when a short maintenance window is acceptable, such as an internal batch component deployed at 2 a.m.

The senior-level nuance is that `RollingUpdate` only delivers genuine zero downtime if three things are true. First, readiness probes must accurately report when a pod can serve traffic, otherwise Kubernetes shifts traffic to a pod that is not ready and users see errors. Second, the application must shut down gracefully, draining in-flight requests when it receives the termination signal, which requires honoring `preStop` hooks and the termination grace period. Third, and most important in banking, database schema changes must follow the expand-and-contract pattern, where you first deploy a schema change that both the old and new code can use, then deploy the new code, then later remove what the old code needed. If you skip this, the overlap window during a rolling update will break one of the two versions.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, two services need deployment during the day. The Transfer API serves customers constantly and must never go down. A separate Settlement Scheduler is a singleton that, once a night, sweeps pending trades and settles them; it must never run as two instances because that would double-settle trades.

Problem 1 — The Transfer API needs a new version deployed at noon with no interruption. If we simply killed all pods and started new ones, customers mid-transfer would see errors. This is exactly the situation RollingUpdate solves: new pods come up and pass readiness before old pods are removed, so traffic never hits a dead service.

Problem 2 — During the rolling update, version 2.3 and version 2.4 of the Transfer API run at the same time for a minute or two. If version 2.4 expected a database column that version 2.3 does not write, one of them would fail. This is exactly why the overlap window demands backward compatibility and expand-and-contract schema changes.

Problem 3 — The Settlement Scheduler must never have two instances active. If we used RollingUpdate, for a brief moment the old scheduler and the new scheduler would both be running and could both settle the same trade. This is exactly why Recreate is the correct strategy for a singleton: the old pod is fully gone before the new one starts.

To make this concrete, we will build a small program that simulates both strategies against a set of pods. It will contain a `Pod` class with a version and a ready flag, a `DeploymentStrategy` interface with two implementations, `RollingUpdateStrategy` and `RecreateStrategy`, and a `Deployer` that runs a chosen strategy and reports, at every step, how many pods are serving and which versions are live. The demo will roll the Transfer API with the rolling strategy and the Settlement Scheduler with the recreate strategy, printing the availability at each step so the trade-off is visible.

The Kubernetes manifests are part of the deliverable:

```yaml
# k8s/transfer-api-deployment.yml  — customer-facing, zero downtime
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: transfer-api
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1          # at most 5 pods briefly
      maxUnavailable: 0    # never drop below 4 ready -> true zero downtime
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: transfer-api
          image: registry.bank.local/transfer-api:2.4.0
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
```

```yaml
# k8s/settlement-scheduler-deployment.yml  — singleton, must not overlap
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: settlement-scheduler
spec:
  replicas: 1
  strategy:
    type: Recreate        # old pod fully dies before new pod starts
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: settlement-scheduler
          image: registry.bank.local/settlement-scheduler:2.4.0
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/deploy-simulator-1.0.0.jar

# Apply the real manifests to a cluster
kubectl apply -f k8s/transfer-api-deployment.yml
kubectl apply -f k8s/settlement-scheduler-deployment.yml

# Watch a rolling update happen live
kubectl rollout status deployment/transfer-api
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the Transfer API starts with four ready pods on version 2.3.0 and is rolled to 2.4.0 with maxUnavailable zero; the Settlement Scheduler starts with one ready pod on 2.3.0 and is recreated to 2.4.0.

Step 1: The Deployer runs the rolling strategy for the Transfer API. It first surges a new pod on version 2.4.0. Now there are five pods, four of version 2.3.0 and one of 2.4.0, all ready. The service availability never dropped.

Step 2: Because maxUnavailable is zero, only after the new pod is ready does the strategy retire one old pod. The count returns to four, now three of 2.3.0 and one of 2.4.0. Throughout this step both versions are live simultaneously, which is why backward compatibility matters.

Step 3: The surge-and-retire cycle repeats three more times. Each cycle adds a new 2.4.0 pod before removing an old 2.3.0 pod, so the ready count oscillates between four and five but never falls below four. Users experience no downtime.

Step 4: After four cycles all pods are version 2.4.0. The rolling update is complete and only one version is now live.

Step 5: The Deployer runs the recreate strategy for the Settlement Scheduler. It immediately terminates the single old pod. Now zero pods are serving and the service is down. This is the deliberate downtime window.

Step 6: Only after the old pod is gone does the strategy start the new 2.4.0 pod and mark it ready. The downtime window ends. At no point did two versions of the singleton scheduler run together, which is exactly the safety property we needed.

Final output:

INFO: retired one old pod
INFO: serving pods ready = 4 | versions live = [2.3.0, 2.4.0]
... (repeats) ...

```text

    start: [2.3.0 ×4] ready=4

      ▼
    [] ready=0 DOWNTIME (but no overlap — safe for singleton)
      │ start new
      ▼

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kubernetes gives a Deployment two built-in strategies for replacing old pods with new ones, and the difference is fundamentally about whether two versions are allowed to run at the same time. RollingUpdate, the default, replaces pods incrementally: it brings up new pods, waits for them to pass their readiness probe, shifts traffic, and only then removes old pods. Because old pods keep serving until the new ones are healthy, users see no interruption. The cost is that for a short window two versions run simultaneously, and you temporarily consume extra memory for the surge pods. I tune it with maxSurge, how many extra pods are allowed above the desired count, and maxUnavailable, how many pods may be missing during the roll; setting maxUnavailable to zero gives true zero downtime at the cost of always needing room for surge pods.

Recreate does the opposite. It terminates every old pod first and only then starts the new ones, so there is a guaranteed downtime window between the last old pod dying and the first new pod becoming ready. The benefit is that there is never a moment when two versions coexist, which is exactly what you need when the new version is incompatible with the old or when the service is a singleton that must never run twice.

I choose between them based on the application. For a stateless, customer-facing service like our Transfer API, where downtime is unacceptable and the new version is backward compatible during the overlap, I use RollingUpdate. For a singleton like our Settlement Scheduler, which sweeps and settles trades once a night and would double-settle if two instances ran together, I use Recreate, accepting a brief outage during an off-hours deploy because the safety of never overlapping is worth it.

The nuance I always raise in interviews is that RollingUpdate only delivers genuine zero downtime if three things hold. The readiness probe must accurately report when a pod can serve traffic, or Kubernetes will route requests to a pod that is not ready. The application must shut down gracefully and drain in-flight requests when it receives the termination signal. And most importantly in banking, any database schema change must follow the expand-and-contract pattern: first deploy a schema change that both old and new code can use, then deploy the new code, then later remove what the old code needed. If you skip that, the overlap window of a rolling update will break one of the two versions, and in a system that moves money that is a defect you cannot afford. So at National Bank of India, zero downtime was never just picking RollingUpdate; it was pairing it with honest readiness probes, graceful shutdown, and compatible schema migrations.

---

keyPoints: Rolling update: gradual replacement, zero downtime
Canary: small percentage first, then full rollout
Rollback: revert to previous version on failure
